## The three transports

| Transport | Used by | Path |
|---|---|---|
| **HTTP** (plugin) | Dashboard fetches, agent HTTP fallback | `POST /api/plugins/<plugin>/<tool>` |
| **HTTP** (built-in) | Dashboard fetches with bearer | `POST /api/agent-tools/<scope>/<verb>` |
| **MCP** | Spawned agents over `mcp-handler` Streamable-HTTP | `POST /api/mcp` |
| **In-process** | Direct TS imports, server actions | `dispatchProjectedTool(...)` (gated) or `tool.fn(input, ctx)` (ungated) |

The HTTP, MCP, and gated in-process paths all go through the same `dispatchProjectedTool` in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/dispatch-projected.ts` (`dispatchProjectedToolStream` for the in-process streaming variant). The same role/capability/quota/timeout/telemetry behavior applies. The raw `tool.fn(input, ctx)` call is the one exception — it bypasses the dispatcher entirely (see [In-process callers](#how-in-process-callers-reach-a-function) below).

> **mcp-handler's SSE transport is disabled.** Only `/api/mcp` (Streamable-HTTP) is live; `mcp-handler` is configured with `disableSse: true`, so a request to `/api/sse` short-circuits to HTTP 404. SSE was turned off because mcp-handler's SSE transport requires Redis (`REDIS_URL` / `KV_URL`) for cross-process pub/sub, which the operator doesn't run. Streamable-HTTP needs no Redis. (`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/_mcp-handler.ts`.)

## How HTTP requests reach a function

The catch-all routes are stupidly simple:

1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/plugins/catchall.ts` receives the request (the Hono host catch-all — migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/plugins/[...path]/route.ts`). It's a **two-step** catch-all: it first tries the in-memory plugin-`apiRoutes` registry (`dispatchPluginApiRoute`) — a plugin can register bespoke handlers outside the projected-tool system; a registry hit returns that plugin's `Response` directly and skips everything below. A registry miss (`null`) falls through to projected-tool dispatch.
2. Looks up the tool by `lookupByHttpPath(req.pathname)` — if not found, 404 (a 404 on a path that matches a *registered* route under a different HTTP method is upgraded to 405-with-`Allow`, since the catch-all shadows the global method-not-allowed hook)
3. Validates the HTTP method against the manifest's `expose.http.methods` (default `['POST']`) — if not allowed, 405
4. Builds a `UnifiedToolContext` from URL spawn params + headers + the host's resolver impls (spawn, secret, projectDir resolver). If no `run` param/header was supplied, a fresh `runId` is generated server-side so `ctx.askUser` / `ctx.publishState` can install — they gate on `workspaceId + runId`. SSE callers had this since T2.2; the JSON path got parity in the pass-9 audit.
5. If `Authorization: Bearer ...` present, resolves it to a principal and tx (no-op for plugins; required for built-ins)
6. Hands off to `dispatchProjectedTool`
7. Maps the resulting `DispatchProjectedResult` to status code + JSON body

The streaming path is the same except step 7 — when `Accept: text/event-stream` is on the request, the response is a `ReadableStream` of SSE events. Each `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` call from the function emits one event. **Replay-on-reconnect** (Last-Event-ID + X-Papercusp-Run-Id) is handled in `handleHttpToolRequestStreaming` (http-projection.ts): when both headers are present and the tool has a replay-buffer hit, it serves the buffered tail, emits `event: done` with `{resumed: true, replayed: N}`, and closes the sink — no re-dispatch (the original run already aborted on disconnect, by design).

## How MCP requests reach a function

Slightly more involved because we use `mcp-handler` as a transport library.

1. `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/transport/index.ts` (Hono `/api/:transport`, migrated off the retired Next.js `app/api/[transport]/route.ts`) wires a `createMcpHandler` server (Streamable-HTTP only, SSE disabled) with `tools/list`, `tools/call`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list` etc.
2. `tools/list` iterates `listMcpProjections(role)` — projection registry filtered by the calling role from URL params. Returns `{ name, description, inputSchema }` for every visible tool.
3. `tools/call` looks up by `lookupByMcpName(name)`, builds a `UnifiedToolContext` (similar to HTTP, but the spawn context comes from the connection URL), and calls `dispatchProjectedTool`.
4. The dispatcher returns; the MCP SDK serializes the result into the JSON-RPC envelope.

Streaming on MCP works via `notifications/progress` — when the client sent a `progressToken` in `_meta`, every `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` becomes one notification. mcp-handler routes those over the open Streamable-HTTP response stream.

**Write idempotency / result replay.** Passing `_meta.idempotencyKey` on a `tools/call` persists the result under that key (`storeMcpResult`) and replays the stored outcome (`lookupStoredMcpResult`) on any retry with the same key, instead of re-firing the tool. This is recovery for a write whose response died on a dropped connection — opt-in per call.

**Per-call keepalive + deadline.** A long/blocking `tools/call` holds the Streamable-HTTP event-stream open but silent, which would otherwise trip the ~60s tunnel/client idle timers. The transport emits a spec-legal SSE comment keepalive on a cadence well under that (default 20s, `PAPERCUSP_MCP_KEEPALIVE_MS`) to reset both timers, and enforces a server-side deadline (default 55s, `PAPERCUSP_MCP_DEADLINE_MS`, set under the 60s `maxDuration`) that returns a clean JSON-RPC error rather than a silent tunnel drop. Both ride the per-request stream — not the disabled Redis-backed SSE transport.

## Slash exposure — the tool catalog as slash commands

`expose.slash` is a third exposure key next to `expose.mcp` / `expose.http` —
but unlike those it is **a catalog projection, not a dispatch transport**
(plan `slash-exposure-tool-catalog-2026-06-12`, D-001). It projects every
MCP-exposed tool onto the MCP **prompts** primitive, so agent clients that
render MCP prompts as slash commands (Claude Code, OMP) surface the whole
session-visible catalog as `/papercusp:tool:<name>` commands. There is no
fifth framing adapter and no new `tool_invocations.transport` value: the
rendered prompt *instructs the agent* to invoke the tool over the session's
existing MCP connection, so role gates, quota, audit, and result formatting
are all inherited from the normal `tools/call` path.

* **Default ON for every MCP-exposed tool** (owner-ratified D-003). Opt out
  per tool with `expose: { slash: false }`, or override naming/description/
  args with an object (`{ slash: { name, description, args } }`). The
  `papercusp-slash-exposure` flag (default enabled) is the global lever.
* **`prompts/list`** serves the static `definePrompt` catalog **plus** one
  dynamic `tool:<mcp-name>` prompt per visible tool — derived from the *same
  role/profile/manifest/allowlist walk `tools/list` uses* (the shared
  `resolveVisibleToolListings` in `_mcp-handler.ts`), so the slash surface
  mirrors the tool surface by construction. The `tool:` prompt-name
  namespace is reserved; `registerPrompt` rejects static prompts there.
* **Arguments**: top-level scalar input fields become MCP prompt arguments
  (advertised `required: false` on the wire so a bare `/command` is always
  invokable; required-ness is annotated in the description). The rendered
  instruction embeds the full input JSON Schema and directs the agent to
  **elicit missing required fields from the user before invoking**, and to
  confirm first for high-tier tools.
* **`prompts/get`** on a `tool:*` name re-checks session visibility, renders
  the instruction, and writes a `slash.prompt_get` row to
  `harness_shared.audit_log` (slash-origin telemetry; the subsequent tool
  call audits through normal dispatch).
* **Codex** doesn't render MCP prompts as slash commands, so Codex launches
  materialize the same projection as prompt **files** in
  `$CODEX_HOME/prompts/tool-<name>.md`
  (`packages/operator-core/lib/slash-tool-prompts-codex.ts`), with
  `$ARGUMENTS` in the supplied-args slot. Those files carry their own
  managed marker, deliberately disjoint from the saved-prompts marker, so
  the two emitters sharing the flat dir never prune each other's files.

Per-tool mechanics (naming, argument derivation, the instruction render)
live in `libs/generic/tooldef/src/slash-projection.ts`.

## How in-process callers reach a function

The projection registry is exported. Any TypeScript module on the server can do:

```ts
import { lookupByMcpName } from '@papercusp/agent-mcp';

const tool = lookupByMcpName('repomix.pack');
if (!tool) throw new Error('not registered');
const result = await tool.fn(
  { target_dir: '/some/path' },
  {
    workspaceId: 'default',
    harnessSlug: 'sheets',
    role: 'architect',
    runId: 'R',
    spawnId: 'inproc',
    log: console.log,
    progress: () => {},
    signal: new AbortController().signal,
    spawn: pluginSpawnImpl,
    secret: secretImpl,
    projectDir: '/some/project',
    stateDir: '/some/project/.papercusp',
  },
);
```

This bypasses the dispatcher — no role check, no quota, no telemetry. Use when you genuinely want to call the function as a function, not as a tool. For consistency, prefer routing through `/api/plugins/...` even from server-side code so gating + telemetry stay uniform.

## The signed URL params

When a request hits an HTTP plugin route or the MCP transport, the framework reads these query params (or equivalent `X-Papercusp-*` headers):

| Param | Required for | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `workspace` | Always | RLS scoping; `app.workspace_id` GUC |
| `harness` | Path-resolving tools | Looks up `projectDir` / `stateDir` via `loadHarnessRegistry()` |
| `role` | Plugin-tool role gate | A canonical `AGENT_ROLES` id (`worker`, `validator`, `scoper`, `architect`, `reviewer`, `debugger`, `operator`, `documenter`, `curator`, `oracle`, `cup`, `mug`, `planner`, `orchestrator`, … through `judge`). The set is **open** — plugins contribute namespaced `<plugin>:<role>` ids (`role-config.ts`). |
| `run` | All non-worker quotas | `window_key = 'run:<id>'` |
| `chunk` | Worker quotas | `window_key = 'chunk:<id>'` |
| `spawn` | Telemetry attribution | Unique per orchestrator spawn |
| `feature` | Optional context | Passed to `tool_invocations.feature_id` for Intel UI |
| `parent_spawn` | Optional Phase 9 lineage | Captured for spawn-of-spawn telemetry |
| `client` | Optional coordination | Per-session coordination / lock owner id (the operator's stable `s-…` spawnId); part of the signed envelope |
| `exp` | **Signature envelope** | Unix epoch seconds; URLs past `exp` are rejected |
| `sig` | **Signature envelope** | HMAC-SHA256 over the canonical sorted other params, base64url-encoded |

The orchestrator bakes these into the per-spawn `.mcp.json` it writes before launching an agent process. The signed-param allowlist (`SIGNED_PARAM_ALLOWLIST` in `spawn-signing-core.ts`) is **nine data params plus `exp`**: `harness`, `workspace`, `role`, `run`, `spawn`, `feature`, `chunk`, `parent_spawn`, `client`. The orchestrator always bakes the five mandatory params (`harness`, `workspace`, `role`, `run`, `spawn`) and conditionally adds up to four optional ones (`feature`, `chunk`, `parent_spawn`, `client`), then **HMAC-signs whatever it baked plus `exp`** so the dispatcher refuses to honor a rewritten role. The agent's MCP client then carries them on every request without the agent ever having to know about them. See [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing) for the full scheme; the minting end lives at `libs/papercusp/packages/orchestrator/src/spawn-mcp.ts:writeSignedSpawnMcp()`.

## Default exposure

If a manifest entry omits `expose.*`, the framework picks defaults:

- `expose.mcp.name` → `<short-pluginName>.<tool.name>` (drops `@scope/` prefix)
- `expose.http.path` → `/api/plugins/<short-pluginName>/<tool.name>`

So `@papercupai/repomix` plugin's `pack` tool gets `repomix.pack` over MCP and `/api/plugins/repomix/pack` over HTTP. You only declare `expose.*` to override these — for instance, to host the same tool at a non-default URL for backwards compat.

If you only set `expose.mcp` and not `expose.http`, the tool is MCP-only. If only `expose.http`, HTTP-only. The framework requires at least one.

## Streaming progress

Both transports thread `ctx.progress(pct, msg?)` through:

```ts
// Tool function
ctx.progress(0,   'starting');
ctx.progress(25,  'fetched manifest');
ctx.progress(75,  'transformed');
ctx.progress(100, 'done');
```

On MCP (when client passed `_meta.progressToken`):
```
notifications/progress { progressToken, progress: 25, total: 100, message: 'fetched manifest' }
```

On HTTP (when client sent `Accept: text/event-stream`):
```
event: progress
data: {"progress":25,"total":100,"message":"fetched manifest"}
```

The function code is identical for both. Tools that don't call `ctx.progress` work fine — the receiver just gets the final result. `ctx.progress` is a thin alias over the more general `ctx.emit` primitive described next.

## Typed event streams

For tools that need richer streaming than `progress(pct, msg)` — LLM token deltas, mid-stream tool-call announcements, parsed sub-results — declare a typed event vocabulary in the manifest and emit via `ctx.emit(name, data)`:

```ts
defineTool({
  name: 'architect.chat',
  args: z.object({ message: z.string() }),
  events: {
    delta:     z.object({ text: z.string() }),
    tool_call: z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),
    cost:      z.object({ usd: z.number() }),
  },
  requirePrincipal: false,
  roles: ['operator'],
  timeoutSec: 600,
  idleTimeoutSec: 120,
  capability: 'harness:write',
  handler: async (input, ctx) => {
    for await (const ev of runAgentChat({ promptText: input.message })) {
      if (ev.type === 'delta')     ctx.emit('delta', { text: ev.text });
      else if (ev.type === 'tool_call') ctx.emit('tool_call', { name: ev.name, input: ev.input });
      else if (ev.type === 'result')    ctx.emit('cost', { usd: ev.costUsd });
    }
    return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'turn complete' }] };
  },
});
```

### Projection table

| Wire | When emit('delta', payload) is called | When handler returns | When handler throws |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HTTP/SSE** (`z.string()` schema) | `event: delta\ndata: <payload as raw text>` (one or more `data:` lines per SSE spec for multi-line) | `event: done\ndata: <ToolResult.content as JSON>` | `event: error\ndata: { code, message }` |
| **HTTP/SSE** (object schema) | `event: delta\ndata: <JSON.stringify(payload)>` | same | same |
| **MCP** | `notifications/papercusp/event { progressToken, event: 'delta', data: payload }` (always JSON-encoded — JSON-RPC carries strings as quoted strings inside the params object) | `tools/call` response with ToolResult | `tools/call` response with `isError: true` |
| **In-process (`dispatchProjectedToolStream`)** | `{ kind: 'event', name: 'delta', data: payload }` (handler-supplied; no transcoding) | `{ kind: 'done', result }` | `{ kind: 'error', error: { code, message } }` |

### Wire format per event — schema-inferred

The framework inspects each declared event's Zod schema at registration time and picks the on-the-wire encoding:

- `z.string()` → **raw text**. The payload is the text; multi-line content gets split into multiple `data:` lines per SSE spec, joined back by `parseSseStream`. Use for high-frequency token streams (LLM deltas, log lines) — no JSON.stringify on emit, no JSON.parse on consume, smaller bytes per frame.
- Any object/union/etc. → **JSON-encoded**. Use for structured events (suggestions, tool_calls, cost summaries).

```ts
events: {
  delta:      z.string(),                              // raw on the wire
  tool_call:  z.object({ name: z.string(), input: z.unknown() }),  // JSON
  cost:       z.object({ usd: z.number() }),           // JSON
  suggestion: SuggestionSchema,                        // JSON
}
```

The MCP transport always JSON-encodes (JSON-RPC doesn't have a raw-text channel inside a notification's `params`); the classification only affects the SSE wire. Clients consuming over MCP see `data: '<the text>'` as a string field; over SSE for the same event, they see `data: <the text>` without quotes.

### Content-type hints via `.describe()`

Any text-based format works through `z.string()` — XML, CSV, YAML, NDJSON, Markdown, plain logs are all just text-shaped on the wire; the framework doesn't care what the bytes inside the string represent. The producer formats, the consumer parses.

When a tool wants to advertise *which* text format it emits, attach a `.describe()` annotation. It round-trips through `tools/list` as the JSON-Schema `description` field:

```ts
events: {
  diff_patch: z.string().describe('application/xml'),
  log_line:   z.string().describe('text/plain'),
  json_token: z.string().describe('application/json'),
  csv_row:    z.string().describe('text/csv'),
}
```

`tools/list` returns `events.diff_patch = { type: 'string', description: 'application/xml' }`. Clients pick a parser off the description. No wire-format change — the SSE event stays `event: diff_patch\ndata: <text>`.

The MCP transport dual-fires when `name === 'progress'`: every `ctx.emit('progress', ...)` (or `ctx.progress(...)` via the alias) produces *both* `notifications/papercusp/event` and the spec-standard `notifications/progress`. Built-in MCP UIs that watch the standard progress channel still get a signal; Papercusp-aware clients also receive the typed-event payload.

### Reserved event names

The framework reserves these wire-level names (`RESERVED_EVENT_NAMES` in `tool-projection.ts`); the `defineTool` `events` generic refuses them at compile time (`UserEvents<T>`) and `registerProjectedTool` re-checks at register time so JSON-manifest plugins also fail loudly:

- `done` — framework auto-emits when the handler returns (payload: ToolResult content array).
- `heartbeat` — `@papercusp/sse` emits every 10s for keepalive (the `sseResponse` default; the tool event-stream catch-alls don't override it).
- `result` — pre-2026-05-12 legacy terminal name; reserved for collision avoidance.
- `chunk` — framework auto-emits when the handler returns a result carrying an `outputRef` (large-output scratch ref).
- `card` — framework-emitted `ctx.askUser` card payloads; cards ride the state channel, so reserving the name keeps a plugin from intercepting another tool's askUser flow (see [Cards](#cards-interactive-mid-run-prompts) below).

`progress` and `error` are intentionally *not* reserved. `progress` is user-emittable via the `ctx.progress(pct, msg)` sugar, which itself routes through `ctx.emit('progress', ...)` — tools declare a schema for it so the wire kind is inferred. The framework auto-emits `event: error` on handler throw, but a handler may also `ctx.emit('error', { message })` mid-stream for non-fatal errors. The canonical case is `runAgentChat` yielding `{type:'error'}` events that don't terminate the stream.

### Discoverability

`tools/list` surfaces each tool's events as JSON-Schema, so clients can render typed event streams without out-of-band knowledge:

```jsonc
{
  "name": "architect.chat",
  "description": "...",
  "inputSchema": { ... },
  "events": {
    "delta":     { "type": "object", "properties": { "text": { "type": "string" } } },
    "tool_call": { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" }, "input": {} } },
    "cost":      { "type": "object", "properties": { "usd": { "type": "number" } } }
  }
}
```

Standard MCP clients that don't know about the `events` field simply ignore it.

### Idle timeout

`idleTimeoutSec` augments the wall-clock `timeoutSec`: the dispatcher aborts the handler when the gap between `ctx.emit` calls exceeds the cap. Catches wedged child processes that have stopped producing output but haven't formally hung. `0` or `undefined` disables.

### Strict-streamable

The HTTP catch-all returns `406 Not Acceptable` if a client sends `Accept: text/event-stream` against a tool that doesn't stream. The exact predicate differs by catch-all:

- The **built-in `/api/agent-tools/*` catch-all** admits SSE when the tool has **any** of: declared `events` (typed event channel), declared `state` (state-shaped, see [`ctx.publishState`](./state-tools.mdx)), or `expose.mcp.streaming === true` (explicit opt-in).
- The **`/api/plugins/*` catch-all** admits SSE only on declared `events` or `expose.mcp.streaming === true`. It does **not** check `tool.state` — plugin tools don't use the framework `state` channel, so a state-shaped plugin tool would still 406 there.

Either way, this prevents clients from opening an SSE connection for a one-shot result. The `state` trigger (built-in path) matters because state-shaped tools need a `runId`-bearing ctx (`ctx.publishState` only installs when `workspaceId + runId` are both present), and the SSE branch is the path that injects a fresh `runId` via `searchParams.set('run', ...)`. State tools that fell through this predicate before the pass-9 fix returned 406 in spite of having a perfectly valid wire shape.

### Cards (interactive mid-run prompts)

Cards are first-class framework primitives — **not** an emergent pattern that piggybacks on `ctx.emit`. The handler calls `ctx.askUser(spec)` and blocks until the user submits, declines, or the run is cancelled. The card payload travels on the **state channel** (`state-snapshot` events on `GET /api/operator/state-snapshot`), not on the per-tool event ring buffer.

```ts
const r = await ctx.askUser({
  prompt: 'Apples or bananas?',
  dataSchema: z.object({ picks: z.tuple([z.enum(['apples', 'bananas'])]) }),
  presentation: { kind: 'radio', options: [
    { id: 'apples', label: 'Apples' },
    { id: 'bananas', label: 'Bananas' },
  ]},
});
// r.action: 'submit' | 'decline' | 'cancel'
// r.payload (when submit): validated against dataSchema
```

The user's click `POST`s to `/api/operator/conversations/:id/card-response`; the card-correlator resolves the deferred and the handler returns the response value to its caller. Tools no longer echo their args back to the client — the response value IS the user's pick.

The wire-level event name `'card'` is reserved at `registerProjectedTool` (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts:RESERVED_EVENT_NAMES`); a tool declaring `events: { card: ... }` throws at register time. This prevents plugins from intercepting `ctx.askUser` flow by name collision on the events channel.

Full reference: [ctx.askUser](./ask-user.mdx). Implementation files: `libs/generic/tooldef/src/{card-correlator,state-channel,workspace-lifecycle}.ts` (the `askUser` ctx wrapper itself lives in the `ctx-bindings` step of `dispatch-stack.ts`) + `packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-route/routes/operator/{state-snapshot,card-response,run-cancel}.ts` (the wire paths are still `/api/operator/state-snapshot` and `/api/operator/conversations/:id/{card-response,run-cancel}`).

## Result formats — token-efficient serialization

A `ToolResponse.data` is no longer always `JSON.stringify`'d into `content[0].text`. The result serializer (`libs/generic/tooldef/src/serialize-result.ts`, the single source of truth for every transport) picks a **token-efficient format** server-side and labels it. Plan: `token-efficient-tool-result-formats-2026-06-06`.

**Format selection (delivered, not requested).** The model never names a format — efficiency is a deterministic server-side choice:

- **Server default** — the MCP transport (the agent-facing surface, where the LLM reads `content[0].text`) defaults to **compact**; every other transport (HTTP catch-all, in-process, IPC) defaults to lossless **JSON**. "Compact" resolves to the best format the data's shape can be safely rendered in: **TOON** for arrays, JSON for single objects. TOON is a JSON-lossless superset that renders uniform arrays as CSV-style rows — ≈ −20–35% tokens on real list payloads.
- **Eligibility** — when a tool declares an output schema (`defineTool({ result: z.array(...) })`), `@papercusp/result-encoding`'s `analyzeSchema` computes the capability set once at registration: a flat array of scalar-only objects → `{json,toon,csv,tsv,md}`; an array with nested/heterogeneous rows → `{json,toon}`; a non-array → `{json}`. No schema → the TOON runtime auto-encoder still gives a compact path.
- **Negotiation override** — set by the *client process*, not the model. HTTP: `?format=` or `Accept` (`application/toon`, `text/csv`, `application/json`). MCP: `_meta.format` on the `tools/call` params, or `?format=` on the connection URL. The requested format is intersected with the tool's capability set; an unsupported request falls back to the best representable format and labels the downgrade (`_meta.formatFallback`).

**The response contract.** Every compact payload self-identifies so the model never parses an unlabeled one:

- `content[0].text` carries the rendering prefixed with a `format: <fmt>` marker (JSON, the assumed default, is left unmarked). TOON additionally carries its own self-describing `[N]{cols}:` header — which is also where the **row count** lives (so list tools drop any `{ ok, count }` wrapper).
- `_meta.format` records the format machine-readably; `_meta.nextCursor` / `_meta.degraded` / `_meta.degradedReasons` carry the pagination/degraded **envelope** — routed OUT of the tabular body so compact formats are safe for paginated list tools.
- `structuredContent` (opt-in via `?structured=1` / `_meta.structured`) carries the lossless structured JSON for UI/programmatic consumers — gated OFF by default so the model never pays for both the compact text AND the JSON.

**Lossless guarantee.** `@toon-format/toon` is lossless in the common case but has round-trip edge cases (pathological keys; certain string values with structural characters in its nested form). The encoder VERIFIES the round-trip (`encodeToonChecked`: encode → decode → deep-compare) and falls back to JSON whenever it doesn't hold — the model is never handed a compact payload that doesn't decode back to the input. See the agent-insight [Parsing tagged compact tool results](/internal/docs/agent-insights/compact-tool-result-formats).

MCP `tools/list` advertises a tool's `outputSchema` (spec-aligned) and a Papercusp `resultFormats` extension (its capability set) so a client knows what it may negotiate.

## Freshness negotiation — `_meta.delta`

Alongside `format`/`structured`/`idempotencyKey`, an MCP `tools/call` may carry a fourth
`_meta` control: `delta` — a per-call value (`req.params._meta.delta`) that wins over a
connection-level `?delta=` on the MCP URL, mirroring the `?format=` fallback. It lets a
delta-capable tool answer `not_modified` (or a semantic `added`/`updated`/`removed` diff)
instead of replaying an unchanged snapshot, mirroring HTTP `ETag`/`If-None-Match`. The
**harness**, not the model, sets this and owns cursor storage + base-presence tracking —
absent ⇒ no negotiation (serve `full`, today's behavior, byte-identical to a delta-unaware
client). Full contract, cursor format, the base-presence rules, and the production
flag/gate: [Tool result freshness: the delta base-presence contract](/internal/docs/agent-insights/tool-delta-base-presence-contract).

## The three context types

The codebase has three context types floating around — same field set, different supersets. Knowing which is which helps when tracing types through the dispatcher and transport adapters.

| Type | Lives at | Used by | Streaming? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `UnifiedToolContext` | `libs/generic/tooldef/src/tool-projection.ts` | The dispatcher canonical context. All transport adapters build one. | Yes — `emit`, `progress`. |
| `ToolContext` (plugin-sdk) | `packages/plugin-sdk/src/index.ts` | Plugin tool handlers (`PluginToolMap`). | Yes — `emit`, `progress` (mirrored from UnifiedToolContext). |
| `ToolContext` (legacy, engine) | `libs/generic/tooldef/src/types.ts` | Legacy principal-gated `defineTool` handlers — `{ principal, tx, log }` only. | No — these don't stream. |

When `defineTool({ requirePrincipal: false, … })` is called (role-gated), the handler receives `UnifiedToolContext` directly. When `defineTool({ … })` is used with default `requirePrincipal: true`, the wrapper synthesizes the legacy `ToolContext` from the unified one — `emit`/`progress` are dropped because legacy built-ins don't stream.

## Trust model

The per-spawn URL params are **HMAC-signed** end-to-end. The orchestrator mints with the shared key in `harness_shared.operator_secrets`; the dispatcher verifies before honoring any role claim. A worker that rewrites `?role=worker` → `?role=operator` produces an invalid signature, the request is rejected with `request_rejected: spawn_sig_invalid_signature`, and the attempt lands in `harness_shared.spawn_sig_verification_failures`. See [Spawn-URL signing](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing) for the full scheme and threat model.

Layered defences still apply:

- The operator binds to `127.0.0.1` (`PAPERCUSP_BIND_HOST` defaults to loopback). Only local processes can hit `/api/plugins/*` or `/api/[transport]`.
- Built-in tools still require a bearer principal when accessed without a spawn ctx. They throw `UnauthorizedToolError` (HTTP 401) when none is present.
- `.mcp.json` is written mode 0600; per-spawn worktree dirs are mode 0700.

The signing scheme defends against prompt-injected workers rewriting URL params. It does **not** defend against same-UID code reading the signing key from PG, replaying another spawn's still-valid URL, or any of the other same-UID escalation paths catalogued in [Spawn-URL signing → Threat model](/internal/docs/endpoint-system/spawn-signing#threat-model). Off-loopback exposure still needs a real principal/auth layer in front; that's separate work.

### Desktop IPC: webview is in-boundary

The desktop Tauri app uses a fourth transport — endpoint IPC over a Unix domain socket (Linux/macOS) or named pipe (Windows). The Tauri webview opens a `Channel<T>` through Rust to the Node sidecar's IPC server (`libs/generic/ipc-endpoint-server/src/server.ts`); the round-trip skips localhost HTTP entirely. See [`packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/PROTOCOL.md`](https://github.com/Papercusp/papercup/blob/main/packages/operator-core/lib/endpoint-ipc/PROTOCOL.md) for the wire format.

IPC calls **skip HMAC signature verification**. The trust boundary is different from the signed-URL HTTP path:

- The signed-URL model defends against a spawned subprocess rewriting its own `?role=...` query param. That subprocess is untrusted code (often a prompt-injected worker) running in a separate process.
- The webview is *not* a separate process in the same threat sense — it's spawned by the same Tauri parent that spawned the Node sidecar, runs the same trusted UI code, and lives in the same process tree. Rewriting "its own role" is a category error: the webview is the role.

So the IPC adapter synthesizes a fixed `principal: { role: 'operator', workspaceId: <active-workspace> }` and dispatches without verifying any signature. The same dispatcher (role gates, rolesQuota, telemetry, idle/wall-clock timeouts) still runs — only the cryptographic verification step is bypassed. All other defenses (loopback bind, file modes, `.mcp.json` permissions) continue to apply.

What this does **not** apply to:

- **MCP-spawned agents** (claude-code / omp subprocesses) — they go through `/api/mcp` (Streamable-HTTP; `/api/sse` is disabled) over loopback HTTP with signed URLs. They're untrusted same-UID code, exactly the threat the signing scheme targets.
- **The non-Tauri webapp** (`:3070` test surface, mobile RN clients) — these are not in-boundary; they use HTTP+SSE.

The transport column in `tool_invocations` records which path each call took (`ipc` / `http` / `mcp` / `in_process`), so post-incident review can distinguish the in-boundary fast path from the signed-URL slow path.
